## Two layers that agree only at the edges

Two rhythmic layers can share a beginning and an ending and argue about
everything in between. Cut a two-beat span in half and each event lasts one
beat. Cut the same span in three and each event lasts `2.0 / 3` of a beat. Run
both at once and they meet at the cycle boundary, then disagree until the next
one.

A *tuplet* fits one number of equal events into a span that normally holds
another number. Three events in the time of two gives you triplet divisions.
Sound the three-part layer against the two-part layer and what you have is a
3-against-2 polyrhythm.

One thing to get right before you run it: that decimal has to come from the
fraction. Type an approximation and the error compounds. Over sixteen cycles a
boundary that should be shared drifts far enough to hear, and the third
variation makes you listen to exactly that.

Play the program once and count the attacks inside a single two-beat cycle.
Four? Five? Six? Write your number down before you read the explanation.

## Sixteen cycles of three against two

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72

in_thread do
  16.times do
    2.times do
      sample :drum_bass_soft, amp: 0.9
      sleep 1.0
    end
  end
end

in_thread do
  16.times do
    3.times do
      sample :elec_tick, amp: 0.75
      sleep 2.0 / 3
    end
  end
end

sleep 32
```

The low drum marks the start and the midpoint of every two-beat cycle. The tick
cuts the same span into thirds. At 72 BPM you have room to follow one layer for
several cycles before switching your attention to the other, which is the way
to learn this texture. Heard together, the two layers form one repeating
composite, and both sounds land together at the top of every cycle.

## Slow it down, speed it up, break the fraction

1. Drop the tempo to 48 and tap one hand with each layer. Keep both hands
   moving through the shared two-beat span. The slower rate gives every
   internal attack room to be placed rather than guessed.

2. Restore the code and push the tempo to 132. Are you still following two
   streams, or has your ear collapsed them into one rhythm? The arithmetic is
   untouched, so anything that changed happened in you.

3. Back to 72 BPM, and replace `2.0 / 3` with `0.67`. Let the whole run play
   out and compare a late boundary against the first one. Per event the error
   is nothing. Repeated addition is what makes it audible.

## Alignment by shared invariant

Each thread runs its own local musical clock. The two-part thread sleeps `1.0`
twice; the three-part thread sleeps `2.0 / 3` three times. Both sums come to
two beats, so the scheduler returns them to the same boundary without either
thread sending the other a single message.

That's concurrency coordinated by a shared invariant, and you've built the
pattern before in other work. Independent workers stay aligned when they agree
on the length of a cycle and nothing else. Here the internal subdivisions are
free to conflict while the boundary holds everything together. Put a quiet
marker on every two beats and the invariant stops being an argument and becomes
something you can hear.

Inside one cycle the combined attacks land at beat 0, at two-thirds, at 1, and
at four-thirds, then both layers return together at beat 2. Four distinct
attack points, with the first one struck twice. Write those fractions down if
the texture blurs. Then mute the tick and follow the drum, mute the drum and
follow the tick, and put both back. Isolation trains your attention, and the
full texture is still what you came for.

Swapping in `0.67` gives each three-part cycle a length of `2.01` beats. A
hundredth of a beat sounds like nothing once. Sixteen cycles turn it into a
displacement of `0.16` beats, which at 72 BPM is around 133 milliseconds of
slippage between two layers that were supposed to coincide. Rounded values are
fine on a label. Repeated scheduling needs the exact expression.

Sonic Pi represents the division in finite floating-point precision too, and
`2.0 / 3` still sits far closer to the intended ratio than any two-decimal
literal you could type. The run is bounded at sixteen cycles, which keeps the
remaining numerical error well below anything this exercise asks you to hear.

Part 4 turns from distance in time to distance in pitch. Lesson 18 puts the
semitone arithmetic from Lesson 2 together with the spelling metadata you
preserved in Lesson 10, because naming an interval takes both at once.

## Sixteen cycles with a marker

Render sixteen cycles of 3 against 2 and add a quiet, distinct marker at the
top of every two-beat cycle. Print the expected total of 32 beats before
anything sounds. Add no corrective sleep to either layer. Their own duration
sums have to produce the alignment on their own.

Check the arithmetic first, including each thread's total. Then audition the
full run in Sonic Pi 5 and compare an early marker with a late one. The last
cycle should open with both layers and the marker together. If the marker
covers either pattern, turn it down: a boundary reference exposes drift, and it
shouldn't replace the texture it's measuring.
